title: Teen Charged Over Alleged Plot to Attack Hindu Temple Near Chicago
excerpt: Police say co-workers reported an alleged manifesto and a jammed rifle on Sunday, leading to the arrest of a 19-year-old Palatine man now held pending trial.
body:
• Alexandros Paporakis, 19, of Palatine, Illinois, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing weapons over an alleged plot against a Hindu temple in Aurora.
  • Prosecutors say an eight-page document he sent a co-worker described Indians, Jews and African Americans in dehumanising terms and set out a plan to kill as many people as possible.
  • Police say a search of his home found an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, ammunition and items bearing Nazi imagery.
  • A judge ordered Paporakis held before trial, with his next court appearance scheduled for October 30; police say they have identified no continuing threat linked to the case.

Police in the Chicago suburbs say they stopped a planned attack on a Hindu temple after the co-workers of a 19-year-old man reported messages in which he described a mass shooting, shared photographs of tactical gear and said his rifle had jammed on the day he allegedly intended to act.

Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from Palatine, Illinois, was arrested on Sunday afternoon as he left his home, in a coordinated operation by Palatine and Mount Prospect police. According to CNN, investigators believe he planned to target the largest Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, while the exact intended location remains under investigation.

What prosecutors allege happened on Sunday

Prosecutors from the Cook County State's Attorney's Office say Paporakis had told co-workers that Sunday would be a special day. Earlier that day, according to prosecutors, he called one co-worker to say his gun had jammed and that he had left the scene quickly without being seen.

He also allegedly shared electronic messages showing an AR-style rifle failing to fire and a photograph of himself wearing a tactical vest. Two colleagues contacted emergency services. That tip, police say, set the arrest in motion on the same day detectives believe an attack may have been planned.

"The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated."

— William Nord, Palatine Police Chief

Palatine Police Chief William Nord said protecting places of worship is a law enforcement priority, according to CNN.

The document and the search of his home

At the centre of the case is an eight-page document prosecutors say Paporakis sent to a co-worker. Its title presented it as an Aurora shooter's manifesto. According to court documents reported by the Times of India and CNN, the document described Indian, Jewish and African American people as "subhumans" and described a plan to kill as many as possible. Prosecutors say the author described himself in it as a white supremacist and neo-Nazi who fantasised about mass murder.

A search of Paporakis's residence found an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines and ammunition, body armour and items bearing Nazi or white-supremacist imagery, according to police and prosecutors. Investigators also recovered a gas canister labelled with a racial slur directed at South Asians. The FBI is assisting in the case, the Times of India reported. Court documents cited by local broadcasters indicate the alleged planning had been under way for two years. It was not immediately clear whether Paporakis has legal representation.

Response from Hindu organisations and police

The Hindu American Foundation welcomed the law enforcement response and urged people to remain vigilant and report potential threats, saying every community deserved to worship without fear. Aurora police contacted Hindu temples in their jurisdiction after they were alerted to the alleged plan. Authorities said they had identified no continuing public threat linked to the case.

For Indian-American families, the practical step from that response is direct: temples have been contacted by local police, and anyone who sees a specific threat should report it to police rather than circulate it only within community groups. The case also arrives during wider concern among community organisations about online anti-South Asian hostility, including rhetoric tied to immigration and the H-1B visa programme. A September report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate, cited by the Times of India, found a surge in online anti-South Asian hate.

What happens next

A judge on Wednesday ordered Paporakis held pending trial. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30. Investigators still have to confirm the intended target, examine the seized weapons and devices, and decide whether additional charges follow. For worshippers in Aurora and the Chicago suburbs, the immediate question is security at upcoming gatherings — and, on the evidence police have released so far, whether a co-worker's decision to call 911 was the point at which the alleged plot stopped.
